utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The Chamber is going to ask Madam Registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, counsel. For the Prosecution, Mr. Daryl Mundis, and I, Ekkehard Withopf, with Ms. Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic, together with my colleague Stefane Bourgon and our legal assistant, Mirna Milanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the accused Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Rodney Dixon, with our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids welcome to all the people present, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused, and the interpreters, which are helping us with the translation, of course, the registry, and Madam Usher. Before calling in the witness, the Chamber is going to respond to the question raised yesterday by the Defence. Just wait a moment, please. The question raised by the Defence. But the Prosecutor wishes to intervene first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification: We are not intending to tender the prior statement into evidence. We only want to use it to refresh the memory of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But nevertheless, the Chamber is going to respond to the questions raised by the Defence. Yesterday, the question raised was the following: Can the Prosecution, during the examination-in-chief of a witness, ask questions while submitting to him at the same time a document drafted during a previous examination? Regarding this important question, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in 90(F), provides for the Chamber to control the modalities of the examination of the witness and the presentation of evidence. So it is the Chamber that controls the modalities. The Chamber must make sure that the procedure is effective for the establishment of the truth, and of course it must avoid any waste of time. Regarding the modalities of the examination, they are not strictly defined in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Nevertheless, 89(F) envisages that the Chamber will apply the Rules of section 3, entitled "evidence" -- "Rules of Evidence." It is also specified that in the case that the Rules are mute, the Chamber will apply such Rules so as to achieve, in the spirit of the Statute and the interests of justice, an equality of arms. Therefore, the Chamber notes that the procedure applied by the Prosecution had as its essential aim, as indicated a moment ago, to refresh the memory of the witness. Actually, the witness was interviewed last year on facts that took place in 1993, which means almost ten years ago, and during the previous case, this evidence was collected four years ago. So of course there is a need to refresh the memory of the witness. The jurisprudence of several common-law countries allows the witness, in order to have his memory refreshed, to have at his disposal notes and allows him also to look at his written statement before his oral testimony. This is the jurisprudence in great Britain, in the United States, and in several common-law countries. What is the practice applied in this Tribunal? On certain occasions, it was allowed to use the testimony collected during a previous interview by the OTP during the examination. However, it should be noted that the Rules are totally silent regarding this issue. Therefore, how can we refresh the memory of a witness without juxtaposing his previous statement? And it is the opinion of the Chamber that the Prosecution has the possibility of communicating with the witness prior to the hearing and can therefore refresh his memory then. And an examination conducted with prudence can also, through its questions, refresh the memory of the witness. Consequently, the Chamber, which needs to control the examination, rules that to the extent to which the examination-in-chief is oral, the previous statement should not be presented to the witness during that stage and be used to possibly correct his answers. Therefore, it is not possible to produce that type of document during the examination-in-chief. Concerning, more specifically, yesterday's hearing, during which the testimony -- or rather, the statement was shown to the witness, the Chamber notes that the question put to the witness had to do exclusively with the signature on the document, his signature on the document. Therefore, the Chamber rules that the Prosecution used this document yesterday strictly respecting the conditions envisaged by section 3 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and therefore, there is no need to further discuss the issue. We will now, therefore, call the witness who testified yesterday and who is going to continue his testimony, unless the Prosecutor wishes to intervene. I am listening. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, just one question. Will there be a written decision following in that respect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent to which the request was made orally, we also respond to it orally. But you can refer to the transcript to see what was said. The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to thank the Trial Chamber for making such a ruling regarding such an important issue at the very beginning of trial, so that this should not be an obstacle during the continued proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification: Does this decision apply for prior statements only, or does it also apply for different documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It only applies to prior statements collected within the framework of an investigation conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor. Other documents, obviously, may be produced during the examination. Madam Usher, will you have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Are you hearing the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Yesterday we completed the examination-in-chief, and now we should begin today with the cross-examination on the part of the Defence. So I give the floor to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am attorney Edina Residovic and I am defence counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I hope you had a good rest and you will be able to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you come from the village of Donja Visnjica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Donji Visnjica was in the local commune of Lasva?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The local commune of Lasva belonged to the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zenica is the largest regional centre in the area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, regional centre?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The centre in the Lasva area.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the centre of the district. Yes, whatever you needed, you went to Zenica, but Lasva really belonged to Busovaca, Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Zupa, you mean the parish, the church parish?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as you said, for anything that you needed, you went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went to secondary school in Zenica too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that for a brief time you were working in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Other inhabitants of your local commune, the village of Lasva and the surrounding hamlets, also went to Zenica for various needs they had?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask the witness to be shown a map. It is Exhibit DH3, to the witness. Can it be shown on the ELMO, please. DH3 is the exhibit number. Could the witness be given a black-and-white version of this same map for the ELMO. Could the technical booth show Exhibit DH3 on the screen, please. As far as I can see, we all can see the picture on the screen, and the witness has an identical map, only in black and white.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you have the black-and-white version of that map next to you. On the screen you have it in colour, and to your side, you have it in black and white. It is the same map. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, would you be kind enough to take a pointer to show for all of us, with greater precision, the things you spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher give the witness a pen or a pointer. Could we have the map on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark on the black-and-white copy of the map Donja Visnjica, that you come from. Could you mark that, if you can see it, with number 1. Number 1. Just put number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with number 2 --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could take you down there and show you everything where all these things happened. As far as the map is concerned, everything is fine. But if necessary, I'll take you down there and show you how everything was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your offer, but I don't think that the Trial Chamber could go on the spot. So could you please show us the things that you know and you recognise on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could now the map on the ELMO be shown for the benefit of all the participants on the screen. I was asking the technical department that to substitute the DH3 map with the black-and-white map that the witness is marking. Could it be shown on the screen, please, with the help of the ELMO. Is that possible now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is what possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm asking the technical booth. Can we see the map on our screen now, the black-and-white map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? At the technical level, I'm afraid there's no technician to manipulate the buttons so it has to be done at the witness box. Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not very good with technical matters, but thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark on the map that you have to your right, with the number 1, the location of Donja Visnjica, if you recognise it. Will you put a number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you point to the place where the railway station is in Lasva. Mark it with a number 2.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the Lasva railway station?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Near the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know where the shop is where your HVO unit had its base or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shop in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be more precise with my question. Next to the Lasva railway station, was there a store?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several. One was an Upi, and there was a coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that shop next to the coffee bar, was that where your HVO unit was based?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did drop in sometimes to have a drink there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map the spot in Lasva where the checkpoint was where you, as members of the HVO, were manning.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way out of Lasva, to the right, where the bus station used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate that on the map and mark it with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you find on the map, and mark with a number 4, the hamlet of Kegelj, in the village of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please find on the map, and mark, the house of Drago Rados at Brdo, just below Petar's [phoen] house. Could you mark that with a number 5 please, on the map.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to tender this marked map into evidence, as it shows the location the witness referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, will you give this an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, is it true that in Drago Rados's house, was the place where the HVO members of Dusina gathered and met, the squad or group?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have met there sometimes. I did what I was ordered. The commanders would be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You just tell me as much as you know. On the map, we saw certain villages and hamlets of your local commune. Tell me, please: Is it true that those villages and hamlets are separated by small hills or hillocks, that they are separated by higher elevations?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Donja Visnjica is in the valley, and then above it, there's Vranica Stijene, and Brdo is also in a valley, and then there's a hill just above it. But then Gornja Visnjica is there to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the Brdo hamlet, it is not possible to see the houses in the Kegelj hamlet because of the hills?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't see them. You can only see the Kalajdzic's houses. No, you can't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the hamlet of Brdo, you can't see your houses in Donja Visnjica and Lasva either, can you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your brother lived in Lasva, near the crossroads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, at the crossroads, the junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That crossroads or junction, whatever you like to call it, is very important for communication towards Travnik, Busovaca, and so on?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, Zenica, Kakanj as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Is it very important?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that after April 1992, in Sarajevo, you couldn't take the main road because the Serb forces had occupied parts that lay south of Visoko?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any need to go to Sarajevo, so I can't really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the block -- if the road via Busovaca were blocked too, would the only way of reaching Kacuni and the parts reaching to Sarajevo, the road via Lasva and Dusina?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on foot or if you're driving in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, both walking or driving. If the road from Kaonik to Busovaca were blocked.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the road across Dusina. As to that other road, there's one going via Lugovi and Gornja Visnjica you can take -- you can walk there and from Dusina where the Bosniak population lives. But I would usually go via Bula [phoen]. That's the road I know best.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the roads you mentioned are mountain roads, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Well, a tractor can move along them too, for example, and horse and cart.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that from 1992 onwards you were a member of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, the 8th of April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You belonged directly to the unit in Lasva, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And your commander was Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your unit, Mr. Batinic, was not a component part of the HVO brigade called Jure Francetic from Zenica although Lasva did in fact belong to Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your superior command was in Busovaca, in fact?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your unit received orders only from your command in Busovaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the commanders know that up there better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified and said that the relations with the BH army deteriorated at the beginning of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Well, there was tension before that too, before the 26th of January, while they stationed themselves at Usce at the mouth we knew what was being prepared but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were aware of the fact that the Main Staff had issued an order according to which combat readiness of all HVO units should be raised to the highest alert, red alert. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we gave the Bosniaks rifles to stand guard together with us. They didn't have any weapons at one point in time. And then afterwards, of course, we had to protect and defend ourselves from them, when the Serbs pulled out from the barracks in Zenica, of course, we gave us [as interpreted] rifles to stand guard with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also issued an order to prevent any movement on the part of the Muslim forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were just defending and protecting - how shall I put this? - our own homes, households, because had there not been a conflict, we would of course stayed there. So yes, we were there to defend and protect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also ordered to take transports of weapons and munitions from the Muslims passing through your area?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, let's go back a little way to the conflict in Busovaca that you mentioned a moment ago. As a unit from Busovaca, you were well aware of the fact that around the 20th of January, armed conflicts broke out between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the 20th of January. It was two or three days before what happened in Lasva took place. And allegedly, the man was killed up there. Was it Ivica Gaj or whatever his name was. And that's when the conflict actually started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those conflicts in Busovaca gave rise to tension in your own villages; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A part of the refugees, the Muslim population, went via Lasva to Zenica, from the Busovaca area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The Croatian population left, those of them who had anyone in Zenica to stay with. And I had my mother and my late father, so I could have sent my people there, but we were too late, so we didn't go there. So we stayed there in our houses when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, not far from your own village lies the village of Merdani; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And from the Kegelj hamlet, this is at a distance of approximately two and a half kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, give or take.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said roughly.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't say roughly when, as I say, Brdo was two or three kilometres away, maybe less, whereas Merdani are further. You have to go via Dolovi and Crni and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Give us a rough estimate, then.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say five kilometres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So Merdani was an exclusively Muslim-populated village, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you know that on the 25th of January, early in the morning, the HVO attacked Merdani by opening artillery fire which could be heard in Dusina and Lasva; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution objects against such a line of questioning. It has to do with the tu quoque principle, which is not a proper defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence, would you please ask questions of the witness which took place after the events he's testifying to. Those were your questions. So the Prosecution feels that those questions are not relevant. So could you concentrate your questions on what the witness testified to in response to questions put to him by the Prosecution. And so your cross-examination must focus on the direct facts testified to by the witness and as to the events of the 23rd of January. You're going on to the 25th of January, which was posterior to that. So this is a valid objection. Therefore, please continue your cross-examination, but focus your questions precisely on the matters covered by the Prosecution which you would like clarification on, or if you're questioning what the witness said in response to the Prosecution's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I continue with my cross-examination, may I be allowed to say something and explain my method of cross-examination, which I have followed so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not the method of defence to which the Prosecution has alleged. On day one, you cautioned us and told us how a cross-examination ought to be conducted, in what direction, also in the direction which is of interest to the Defence. I am the Defence counsel for an army general and corps commander, and that incorporates 24 communes and has 16 brigades. It is the position of the Prosecution that the Bosniak forces attacked this village. There are -- the series of questions that I am posing speak of the context and situation in which a high-ranking commander is operating. So the strategy of combat operations, the way -- the reason why they are being conducted is in direct context to the questions that I am asking. So I should like to ask you, Mr. President, to allow me to ask certain questions in that regard and within that framework. I shall now go on and follow your instructions and guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You know that according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, if a question gets far away from the principle matter, the authorisation of the Trial Chamber must be demanded in order to go ahead with questions of that type. But I now give the floor to the Prosecution. Let me just say that the Defence has been asking to ask its questions of the witness with regard to the general context, as it has to do with command, and so the Defence would like to know if the unit that the witness was a member of received orders or not, and if that unit participated in other combat. Because we have learnt that on the 25th of January, that is to say, two days after the fact, there was artillery fire in a certain locality. So the Defence would like to receive confirmation from the witness of that fact, so that is in the more general context. So it is at the level of this general context that the Defence is asking that particular question or line of questioning. So does the Prosecution have any objections to make with respect to context?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution has an objection and in response to what Defence counsel just said. The Prosecution defined the scope of the examination-in-chief at the very beginning of the examination-in-chief to the murder of Zvonko Rajic and to the mistreatment of the witness in the Zenica music school. The questions Defence is about to ask are going far beyond this defined scope.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but they don't extend your guidelines and restrictions and Rule 90(H), which controls the mode of cross-examination and the direction it takes. So I wanted to explain to you the context of my line of questioning so far. And I shall continue with my questions, which have to do with the 26th of January now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the 26th of January can concretise the general context of events that took place on the 23rd, then the Chamber authorises you to ask questions with respect to the 26th of January. Of course, I would like to indicate to the Defence that the witness on several occasions did answer by saying that he was a simple witness and that with respect to command matters, strategic matters, and so on, that was over his head. He has said that several times. So of course you can ask him questions, but his level of competence as being a simple soldier is such that you run the risk of asking questions to which he cannot answer. But anyway, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you said that on the 26th, in the morning, you were in the house of Rados Drago?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Drago. Perica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rados Perica is Rados Drago's brother, is he?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cousins. Anyway, they're related.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So their houses are close by in the hamlet of Brdo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Together with you in the same house was Ivo Filipovic and Srecko Kristo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Ivo Filipovic was there. Just a moment, please. Yes, Srecko was there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else there with you in Rados Perica's house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Perica, there was myself, there was Srecko, and the others turned up later. Rados, Drago was in his own house, spending the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In Drago Rados's house, were there any other HVO members there on that particular morning?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was there alone. Drago Rados was alone in the house while the fighting was taking place and he was in his own house throughout that time because he stayed on there he left us and he spent the night in that house and happened to be there when we surrendered and decided to leave together. That's when he came out of his house. I'm referring to Drago Rados.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic, you said, came one hour later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an hour, hour and a half later. He didn't come alone. Some others came with him. I didn't count how many. But they came together with Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who came with Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers. Do you want names now? Do you want names or what? I can't remember all their names. There was Jozo Kristo, Kreso.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brane.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, from the house you were in, you were able to see the road leading towards the Rados houses, the road leading towards the hamlet of Brdo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, explain this to me, what you mean. Which road?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between the Bosniak houses and the houses belonging to the Rados family, there's a small village lane.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the village lane goes towards Dolovi and as you come down towards Perica and Drago Rados's house there's another steep slope.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether, from the house you were in, you could see that lane leading towards Dolovi?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but the house has -- how shall I say, a veranda, a terrace and there's a window there and you can see Rados Pero's house from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After Zvonko Rajic and the group of HVO soldiers arrived, along this lane you saw a group of BH army members coming towards you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure about that, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw a soldier of the BH army killed from a sniper, and this was in front of Rados's house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. The Bosniak soldier, I think his name was Candzic, he died in battle. Perhaps I killed him. I'm not sure. But there was shooting going on. And had he not attacked, he wouldn't have lost his life. But I'm not quite sure that he was killed from that. And you could have investigated that. You could have examined the bullet and established who had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With Zvonko Rajic, did Zeljko Cvijanovic come with him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that. I don't know. He knows best whether he went there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at that point in time, you didn't happen to see Zeljko Cvijanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people did come up there via Drljaca and they didn't even come to see us, report to us, all of them. And when they saw us surrender, some of the others withdrew and went back down. There's another little lane there, and they went down to Donja Visnjica, some of them, whereas some of them went down with us, of course. So those of us who fought up there were supposed to go down and reach an agreement, and others joined us on the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally know Zeljko Cvijanovic from Lasva, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do know him. He was a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you knew that he was the only person with an Austrian Winchester sniper?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, an Austrian sniper. Well, sometimes he'd carry it around with him. How can I explain this? Now, whether he was issued it or wasn't issued it, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that he was the only one of all you HVO soldiers who had that particular rifle?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. No, no. I'm not sure. If I were sure, I would tell you exactly, but I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether other soldiers had that same type of rifle, like the one that Zeljko Cvijanovic had?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. Thank you. You also told us that at one point in time, Zdravka Rados, the wife of Drago Rados arrived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that from the direction of Dusina she came accompanied by Edin Hakanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a civilian was with her. Edin stayed down there but she came up to us and said, "If you don't surrender they'll kill the civilians."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far from you is that field where Edin Hakanovic remained?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were with up there where the plum orchard is, the plum trees belonging to -- well, as the crow flies -- just a moment. Let me think. Five hundred metres. Yes, five hundred, I would say, as the crow flies, in direct line. But if you go through the field, there's a depression there and the fields they were in were Bosniak fields. Well, two, three hundred metres. I'm not quite sure as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it could be two to three hundred metres as the crow flies, you say.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zrvanje was the name of the field at Vodica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the place you were at, you were not able to hear what those civilians were talking about with Edin Hakanovic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Zdravka Rados came up to you, she said -- she only said that you weren't to shoot because the Muslim soldiers wanted her to convey a message to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zdravka Rados shouted out to you and told you not to shoot, because she said she wanted to come up to you, because she had a message for you, that the Muslim soldiers were sending to you.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and she did come. But we had stopped shooting before that. We shouted out to each other and we stopped shooting before that, and she came up to us. We saw her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew Edin Hakanovic before the war?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We were schoolmates. We went to school together, primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were able to recognise him from that distance from where you saw him., you said approximately two hundred metres as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Zdravka Rados also told you that Edin Hakanovic was down there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember whether she actually said that or not now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic negotiated with Edin Hakanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A man came from down there - I can't remember his name now - and we withdrew straight away. I'm not altogether sure who he talked to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you said yesterday that it had been agreed that the clips be taken out of the rifles, well, not charges, clips. Yes. Yes, clips. And that the rifles be placed on the shoulders and the clips in your pocket, the magazine clips in their pockets and that you were to move to the school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were joined at that point by Drago Rados, who set off together with you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came out of his house and joined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the place you were at, were there some HVO soldiers who stayed on there when you left?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, there weren't any. But perhaps there was somebody in front of the house. Everybody left the house. I don't think anybody stayed on, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see anybody --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't stay, because we all went together and the Bosniak soldiers were the ones who remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as you know, Zeljko Cvijanovic didn't stay there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The body of the killed Candzic was somewhere in front of the Rados houses, is that right, on the road?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where he was, but we did carry it until the army or whoever came to take it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the locality of Vodica, as you said, Vodica, you were informed that there were HVO ambushes and the request was made that certain HVO soldiers, together with members of the army, go forward to check that out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's just one of our soldiers who went there, Mijo Ljubicic. He went down there to inform our soldiers to leave their weapons and to gather at one spot and then we would go together to the Ivo Lola Ribar Elementary School. And then when we got to Vodica, there was a report, they had received a report that it was not possible to go down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was reported, actually, that in Donja Visnjica there was an HVO ambush; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That these soldiers of the 7th Muslim would be captured. Now, who reported that, I don't know. I suppose their command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was only after that report that the army soldiers asked you to surrender your weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't surrender; it was taken by force. They took our weapons by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So soldiers of the army seized your weapons when they heard that there was an ambush in Donja Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if that hadn't happened, maybe things would have happened differently. Who knows?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that at one point in time, Zvonko Rajic tried to escape; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then several soldiers of the army opened fire at him, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three or four of them who were there. Not of the army. The 7th Muslim. They were all together under the command of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you certainly saw and heard that several bullets were fired in the direction of Zvonko Rajic by several soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that after Zvonko Rajic's death, soldiers of the army tied you up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the killing of Zvonko Rajic? Yes, they tied us up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was only after Zvonko Rajic had tried to escape and when he was killed that you were tied up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said, Mr. Batinic, that when you reached the school in Lasva, you saw troops and civilians.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to the Lasva school. I was going through Dolovi, Polom, the rail tracks, the Usce and the music school. I didn't see the school that day at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Lasva?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lasva is in the other direction. We took another route on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So never for a moment did you pass through Lasva by the school and railway station?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of January, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the soldiers who were escorting you, you also came across a part of the civilian population and other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't come across civilians. When a -- a couple only when they went from Crna, we -- they were going from Polom we met them at Dolovi. But we didn't meet civilians. We saw them at the mouth of the river when we waited to be transferred to the music school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that for a moment you saw Batan, your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my neighbour. He escorted us from Brdo to the confluence of the two rivers. Because those who came from the outside didn't know the road, didn't know the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Batan was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had probably given his uniform to someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Batinic. Let us go back. You also told me that your brother had a house close to the Lasva crossroads. Do you know that after the fall of Jajce a large number of refugees reached the area, both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That house wasn't his house. He got an apartment from his company there. And Croats and Bosniaks came from Jajce and settled in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They settled in the abandoned houses in the area, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The houses abandoned by the Serbs. The Croats took those houses. They came from Jajce and Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were saying yesterday how you arrived at the music school, you said that some men would go there, some local people.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One man would come in, a neighbour. I don't have to name him. He was a Muslim. And he recognised me, but I didn't recognise the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Many of them were not in uniform, so they took parts of your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not this one, but the others did. All those who were guarding us down there, they took our boots, vests.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know most of them, nor did you know which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the music school, they belonged to the 7th Muslim. That I know. As for those who came, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So while you were in the music school, some other men entered wearing civilian clothes, and some in uniform, that you didn't recognise?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some gave us cigarettes. Some were good guys. We are not all the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, I should now like to ask you something else. You know that in the canton court in Zenica, proceedings are ongoing against your neighbour, Edin Hakanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The court called you to testify in that court in May 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the investigating judge who interrogated you was Ahmetovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, Ahmetovic. Go on with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be given his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something in that connection, please? May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to the Court, up to the Chamber to decide, so don't ask me. The statements are both in English and Bosnian. Here's a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you personally signed this statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Ahmetovic, before you made your statement, cautioned you that it is your duty to tell the truth and that you would be held responsible for perjury.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But may I say something? I wasn't in a mentally good condition at the time. I'm better now. I feel better. I'm well now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The judge also called your wife, Lidija, to testify about your mental condition.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my former wife. She is not my wife any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the time that for some time you felt psychologically unstable and that you simply don't remember anything any more; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that I didn't remember. I told the judge. He called me -- let me see. Why did he call me? Whether I had seen Hakanovic down there in the meadow, and I told him then that I wasn't sure whether I had seen him. But now I remember. I'm fine now. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you told the judge that you didn't see Hakanovic Edin on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what I have been saying here these past few days, of that I'm 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, your former wife stated that you had some psychological problems for four years prior to that hearing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that hearing, for four years, you can't say that. How could you say that? I was a member of the Army of the Federation. How could I have been a member if I hadn't been mentally all right? Because a soldier has to be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you're undergoing treatment, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm treating myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender this statement too into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, regarding the admission of this document, which was produced during the cross-examination by Defence counsel. Is there any objection against the admission of this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, we are going to give this document an exhibit number, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is DH7, and the English translation is DH7/E.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Batinic, when you were examined by the judge, though you were cautioned to tell the truth, you were not telling the truth about the events?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you tell me what is the falsehood that I uttered? Just ask me a question and tell me which was not -- what was not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you told the judge that you don't remember any of the events that you experienced in the past war?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered, but I couldn't remember all the details. But now I remember everything. I can again repeat a hundred times the things I said yesterday and today, because that is how they were, how they happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is a quarter past 10.00. We would normally adjourn at 10.30 for a break, but I assume that the Prosecution has some questions in re-examination, so I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless, of course, Mr. Kubura's defence wishes to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Like the previous witness he only deals with matters prior to the 1st of April, 1993, which is the time when Mr. Kubura is not charged for any incidents before that time. No questions for him on behalf of Mr. Kubura. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So I give the floor to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this case we have no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, the testimony of Mr. Batinic is over. The Chamber wishes to thank this witness for coming and for testifying and for answering the questions of both the Prosecution and the Defence, and we wish you a happy journey home, and we hope you will be able to catch your plane. Thank you. Madam Usher, will you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, is there another witness has been envisaged? Has he arrived? Is there a delay? We haven't been informed of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we anticipate that the witness will arrive at Schiphol airport in 15 minutes. We anticipate that it will take the witness at least one hour and a half, if not even longer, to arrive here at The Hague. We anticipate that the witness will be available for his testimony at some point in time after noon today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally the hearing was scheduled until 1.45 p.m., so if he arrives in the afternoon, that will be after the hearing. Unless you are suggesting that we could continue the hearing, but unfortunately, this afternoon the courtroom is occupied by another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you sure that he will not arrive before 1.45? Because we can wait up until that time without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We anticipate that the witness will be around about 12.00 or 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we can begin with the examination and continue it tomorrow, in view of these material facts, can the Defence wait until noon for the witness to arrive? No problems? Very well. We are going to adjourn, and as soon as the witness arrives, the Prosecutor will inform us and we will resume the hearing when the witness arrives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I wish to specify that for practical reasons, it would be best for everyone to come back at noon. If the witness arrives earlier, you will be informed; if not, we'll all be here at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before bringing the witness, I will have two remarks to make. Yesterday, the Defence conveyed to us that it provided the registry with documents, and the documents were returned to them because they couldn't be translated. I therefore ask the Defence when it intends to produce documents, to indicate to the Registry that they are urgently needed, because they are to be produced in the debate and that they should have priority for translations. And if you do so early enough, because normally you know which documents you intend to tender, please tell the Registrar that these documents will be tendered into evidence, and then, of course, they will translate them straight away. This is simply to facilitate things and to avoid being in the situation we were in yesterday when we had to wait for the translation of a document to decide whether we would admit it or not. That is my first remark. The second has to do with the Prosecution. You told us the day before yesterday, or yesterday - I don't quite remember - that you intended, in January, to call an expert witness who is a general. As you know, in accordance with Rule 94 bis, when an expert witness drafts a report, that report has to be given to the Defence, and I understand that you did so. But then also the Chamber needs to fix a time period for the Defence to make any observations, if it has any, in accordance with the provisions of 94 bis, to inform the Chamber whether it accepts the statement, whether it wishes to cross-examine, or if it challenges the quality of the expert or the competence of the expert. Therefore, I give you up to the 12th of January, 2004, to let us know what your observations are regarding the expert testimony and the report of the expert witness. Do we agree? So we are now going -- yes, please, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we understand and fully agree with the time limits. We would just like to ask the Prosecutor to provide us with this expert report in the Bosnian language as well, as soon as possible, so that our client, General Hadzihasanovic, could work on it with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand, this report has not yet been served on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the report has been served twice to the Defence some weeks ago, without the signature of the military expert, about a week or so ago with the signature of the military expert. It's exactly the same expert report, urgent translation into B/C/S has been requested. It will be available in the very near future and it will be handed over immediately once available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it will be ready about when?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We anticipate within the next eight to ten days, the translation into B/C/S I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Because according to Rule 94 bis, as soon as the Defence has been served with the report, it has 30 days to convey its remarks. So we were saying about the 12th of January, because this expert has been envisaged for the 16th, 17th, or 18th of January, I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's the 26th to the 28th of January, if needed, for three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So the 26th. So that corresponds to the Rules. So I give you until the 12th of January, 2004. Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have already informed you that we'll be filing a request for the assessment not to accept the statement of our client in the Blaskic case. The expert report relies considerably on that statement, and that is why we wish to underline once again that we will very shortly file this motion so that our objections regarding the expert report will be linked to the determination of the Court regarding the acceptability of our client's testimony in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that point, which has already been raised but not formally, as we don't have a motion, does the Prosecution envisage redacting from the report everything that has to do with the previous statement of the accused? Because the Defence is announcing its intention to file a motion to -- not to accept the prior testimony of our client. So the question to the Prosecution is whether, in order to save time, the Prosecution intends to redact the paragraphs referring to this previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution does not intend to redact such portions of the witness statement. First of all, it's the expert's witness report; and secondly, as we already announced in the course of the Pre-Trial Conference, once the motion is filed, we will respond to enable the Trial Chamber to make a considered legal decision on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that once the motion has been filed, we will have the response of the Prosecution, and there is a risk that the witness will not be able to come on the 26th of January, unless a decision is made in due time. In that case, we will have to postpone that witness to a later date, because we're already in December. Time will be needed for the motion, the response to the motion, the Chamber to decide on a matter of such importance regarding previous testimony. It's quite probable that the 26th of January will not be the date when the witness will be able to be heard. Therefore, this may even go to the Appeals Chamber, and in that case, this expert witness will not be heard on that date. Do you follow the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I certainly do. We understand the problem. However we invite the Defence file to file its motion at the earliest opportunity so we can respond very soon and in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence will only file it once it has the B/C/S translation, so it depends on you again. So as you're saying that we will have it in ten days, that will be the 14th or 15th of December by then, so we really do have a problem there. And therefore, I believe that it will be difficult to hear that witness on the 26th of January. Yes you have the floor if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can the Prosecution make it quite clear: In general, Dr. Reinhardt, in his report, refers in one small section to the previous testimony of the two accused. It is easily excisable from the report. It is only part of the basis on which he forms his opinion, and in the Prosecution's submission he can still give his opinion with or without that in. He can be questioned either way: Would that have affected your opinion? And he can still give his testimony in accordance with the timetable. In the Prosecution's submission, it doesn't matter whether that portion is in or out of his report. But the Prosecution is not in the position to redact it because it is not the Prosecution's -- it's the Defence's -- sorry -- it's the expert's report, not ours, not ours to touch. If Your Honours have decided before, it goes out, we just say we don't rely on that. If Your Honours haven't, I'm sure we can deal with it as we go without worrying about the Appeals Chamber. Because if it goes to the Appeals Chamber, the experience has been it can be many, many, many months before such an issue is decided. So in the Prosecution's submission, the expert can give his evidence, either with or -- in or out. It doesn't matter that much to the Prosecution as to whether it's in. The actual use which may be made of that evidence and how it can be used is a different matter to whether or not the Prosecution -- whether or not the expert has used it in coming to part of his opinion. The Prosecution may be submitting that the evidence which the accused gave in other cases can be used against them on the question of guilt. We may be. That has nothing to do with Dr. Reinhardt's report. It's just one of the matters, the fact that they've said something is just one of the matters which the expert has looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The solution to me appears to be found in Rule 94 bis(B)(iii). It says: "If the parties challenge" - in this case, the Defence - "the qualifications of the witness as an expert or the relevance of all or parts of the report, and if so it will indicate which parts." Then being informed by the challenge of one party, the Chamber may order the redaction of the passages in question. When those passages will be excised from the report. And the Prosecution will question its witness only on the basis of paragraphs which have not been redacted and will not be able to ask questions on the passages left out. Would that suit the Defence? To avoid all loss of time. Because, as you know, you also have to contribute to the efficiency and the speedy nature of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we also do not wish unnecessarily to delay the proceedings, nor to postpone the hearing of the witness, and that is why we fully agree with your suggestion. At the same time, we should like to inform the Trial Chamber that within five days after receiving the Bosnian version, we will officially be filing a motion not to allow the use of our client's testimony in other proceedings in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So then we will wait for that motion and we will certainly find a solution that will be satisfactory for both the Defence and the Prosecution. Can we have the witness brought in now, please, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, would you first tell me whether you can hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, will you give me your name and surname, please, first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milica Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 21st of August, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment I'm working as personal assistant to the European mission of the police in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your domicile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mother and father live in Busovaca, so I spend my weekends there, but I have an apartment in Sarajevo, so I haven't got an actual domicile or residence, home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now, please, take the solemn declaration that you're being shown by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. The Prosecution is going to start off by asking you questions, and we shall have to adjourn the hearing at 1.15. So we have 45 minutes, or rather, the Prosecution has 45 minutes. And if it takes 45 minutes, then we can perhaps end today and have the cross-examination as well; if not, then the witness will have to come back tomorrow. But let me give the floor to the Prosecution for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Kegelj, I'm going to ask you some questions about what happened in Dusina in January 1993, and some experiences you had as an interpreter for the ECMM in 1993 in your meetings with General Alagic. First, in January 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was living in a joint household with my parents and brother in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you working at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To facilitate proceedings, I intend to tender into evidence, Your Honours, two large photographs of the village of Dusina, one being an overhead shot and the other being a closer-in shot. I've shown the photographs to the witness in the few moments I had to speak to her before coming into court, and I have two large blown-up photographs which I can give to Your Honours and we have the others which will be in Sanction, which will be on the screen. We don't have seven copies of this and it will be very unlikely we'll be able to fine seven large colour photographs of this. So if Your Honours are content with that for the moment, I'll proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please hand the photograph to us. Show it to the Defence first and then bring it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour's microphone isn't on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, will you please place the photographs on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, they are -- I can activate those in Sanction and show the witness and everyone at the same time. I will come to that -- if Your Honours can excuse me, I will come to that in a moment. I also -- the Prosecution also wishes to tender into evidence at the moment a large map of the Central Bosnia region, which I will also use with this witness. I have one large mounted copy for the Court and the requisite number of photocopies for everyone else here of the map. It's following the Prosecution's Pre-Trial numbering system, it is PT1502 in our pre-trial exhibit list numbering system. If Your Honours wish to follow that, it would be Exhibit number P1502. So I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar will give us a number. Madam Registrar, can you give us a number for the big map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And so that the record is clear as to what we've tendered, the Prosecution has tendered a composite of three maps which are series 473, 474, and 475 of Travnik, Zenica, and Bugojno, with a cross-section across all three, which covers all the crime scenes alleged in the third amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Kegelj, you told us that you were living in Dusina in January 1993. We're going to put a photograph on the screen which will be -- I apologise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask my learned colleague of the Prosecution, before he commences his examination-in-chief of Ms. Kegelj, to tell us when these photographs were taken of Dusina, which we have just been shown, because the events in the indictment are dated 1993, and we don't know when these shots were taken. So could the Prosecutor inform us thereof. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They were taken by the Dutch forensic crime-scene people from a helicopter in April 2002. Unfortunately, we don't have any contemporary photographs of Dusina. This is to show where things were, as opposed to the state of things in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour has -- the registrar has given one exhibit number. There are actually two photographs. I wish to refer to them separately. Do Your Honours wish them to have two exhibit numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As we actually have three documents, the big map plus two photographs, the big map is P1, one of the photographs taken from the helicopter can be said to be P2, and the third, P3 perhaps, so that we can find our way. And there is reference made at the top of the photograph. One of them says 8966. That will be P2. And the other photo with the number 8969 will be P3. So we have three documents. P1 for the big map; P2 or the 66, 8966; and the 8969 will be P3, so that everybody can find their way in the documents. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P2. It should come up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Kegelj, can you please identify for the Court, by pointing, and I'll do the commentary as we go, as to which -- first of all, is that the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is that where you were living in 1993, January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the house in which you were living in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please point to it? And when you point to it on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: [In English] Just here? [Interpretation] It's this one here. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It might be, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps a pencil for the witness. What I was saying was: Madam Usher, could you please give the witness a pencil so she can mark the place her house stands. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We only have one copy at the moment, Your Honour. That's the copy which you have. If she marks on this one, which is the master -- it would be better if she marked it on a photocopy. Perhaps if she describes it at the moment and we can mark it on later. If there's any dispute with the Defence, it can be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, this is the house belonging to my parents, in which I lived. Actually, the light one here. That's where we lived. And this is the new one that's still under construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And for the record, you're indicating the house in the top left of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, that's right. That's the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Leave the map there for the moment. I'm going to ask you about what happened on the 26th of January, 1993. If the usher could perhaps stay there while you describe and I'll get you to point to things on the map so you can show us what happened and where you went and so on. Did you spend the night on the 26th -- or 25th of January, 1993 in your house in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely how it was. As I said, the night between the 25th and 26th, I spent in my house, together with my family, just like the other local inhabitants, or rather, my relatives and neighbours and uncles and so forth and their families. Early on the morning of the 26th, sometime around 5.30 on my watch is 5.25, I was woken up by a bullet which whizzed through the room I was sleeping in. And then I realised that there was a lot of shooting to be heard outside. I went out of the room. I found my mother and father awake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there? What is your mother and father's name?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: My mother's name is Jela Kegelj and my father's name is Jozo, of course Kegelj being the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from you and your mother and father, were there any other people staying in your house that night?

utterances.speaker: MILICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: That night my brothers were not in our family house, because at the time, they were standing guard, on watch, and they were in one of two Serbian houses which had been abandoned and which can be seen on the photograph -- cannot be seen on the photograph.
